title: Contention: when everyone wants the last one
dek: The last plate of biryani, seat 14C, a shared wallet: when many requests change the same thing at once, code that reads and then writes sells it twice. Here is how to let the database pick one winner, when to lock and when to retry, and what to do about one very hot item.

items: Contention is many requests changing the same thing at once. Code that reads a value and then writes a new one oversells, double-books and loses updates.
Let the database decide in one step: a conditional update, a unique constraint or a row lock. Use version numbers when conflicts are rare and locks when they are common.
When people take minutes to pay, hold the item with an expiry instead of locking it. For one very hot item, line the requests up in a single queue.

body.cap: Reading and then writing leaves a gap in which another request reads the same value. A single conditional update has no gap: the database applies it to the row one request at a time.

items: Lost update: two requests read the same balance, both add to it, and the second write wipes out the first. One of two top-ups vanishes.
Overselling: both requests see one plate left, and both buy it.
Double booking: both see seat 14C free, and both book it.
None of this shows up when you test alone. It appears at 8 pm on a sale day, when requests for the same row arrive within milliseconds of each other.
Conditional update: `UPDATE items SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 7 AND stock > 0`, then check how many rows changed. One means sold; zero means sold out.
Unique constraint: a unique index on (show_id, seat_id) in the bookings table makes a second booking of the same seat fail, however the code around it is written.
Row lock: `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` inside a transaction locks the row until commit, and the next request waits. Use it when the decision needs several reads first, and keep the transaction short.
Stricter isolation: at SERIALIZABLE, PostgreSQL detects these races itself and aborts one of the transactions, which you retry. It is the safest setting and costs some throughput.

body.label: Two ways to handle conflicts
head: Compared
Optimistic: version numbers
Pessimistic: locks
rows: Read the row with its version; update `WHERE id = 7 AND version = 12`; if no row changed, someone else got there first, so read again and retry
Lock the row first; everyone else waits until you commit
Conflicts are rare: editing a profile, a menu, a document
Conflicts are common: the last few seats, a busy wallet
Wasted work and retries when conflicts do happen
Waiting, and deadlocks if two requests lock rows in different orders
Works well: send the version as an ETag and check it with If-Match
Never hold a lock across requests; only inside one transaction

body.cap: A hold with an expiry ends by itself. Nobody has to remember to release the seat, so an app that crashes mid-payment can't keep it forever.

items: When choosing and paying take minutes, don't lock a row that long. Mark the item held, with an expiry, in one conditional update.
The hold ends in one of two ways: payment turns it into a sale, or time runs out and it's free again.
Show held items as unavailable, and show the person holding one how long they have left.
If a payment arrives after the hold expired and someone else took the seat, refund it automatically. It is rare, and it will happen.

body.x: In a flash sale, 1 lakh people want the same 500 phones in the first second. Thousands of conditional updates on one row wait for its lock in turn, and the database spends its time on that row while every other order waits. Ways out:

items: Queue the requests, in a queue or one partition of a log, and let one worker sell the stock in order. Customers see 'you're in line' and get the answer a moment later.
Split the stock into buckets, say 10 rows of 50, and send each request to a random bucket that still has stock.
Keep the count in memory, in Redis with an atomic `DECR`, and write orders to the database behind it. It is fast, but plan for Redis failing halfway through the sale.
Turn most requests away early, with a waiting room or a lottery for the right to buy.

body.x: When the thing to protect isn't a database row, such as 'only one worker pays this restaurant', you need a distributed lock: a lease with an expiry in Redis, etcd or ZooKeeper. A holder can stall (a long garbage-collection pause, a slow network) past its expiry while someone else takes the lock. So hand out a fencing token, a number that grows with each new lock, pass it with every write, and have the storage refuse writes with an older token. The ZooKeeper component shows how a lock service hands out these tokens.

items: Name the contended thing out loud: the seat, the stock, the wallet.
Pick the mechanism: a conditional update or a unique constraint for one row, a hold with an expiry when paying takes minutes, a queue for one very hot item.
Say what the loser sees: 'sold out', 'someone just took this seat', or a quiet retry.
Mention idempotency: a retried 'buy' must not buy twice.

body.x: Two transactions each lock one row and then wait for the other's row, so neither can go on. Databases notice this and abort one of them, which then has to retry.

items: Lock rows in the same order everywhere, for example by ID, so two transactions can't wait on each other in a circle.
Keep transactions short, and never wait for a network call or a person while holding a lock.
